output.title: Start with the exception queue
output.body:
Before you automate a workflow, name the exception queue first. That is the pile of work that falls outside the main path: customer questions that need a different answer, invoice mismatches, data corrections, or similar cases that keep interrupting the day. If you cannot point to the queue, you probably do not understand the work well enough to automate it cleanly.

The useful question is not “can AI do this?” It is “what happens when the main rule does not fit?” For one week, track one queue in plain language: how many exceptions arrive, how long each one takes to resolve, and what rule the team uses to decide the outcome. Then sort the queue into three buckets: routine, mixed, or ad hoc. Routine exceptions are the clearest candidates for a narrow pilot. Mixed queues still need human review built in. Ad hoc work usually stays manual because the pattern is too thin.

Keep the control rules visible. If the queue touches approvals, thresholds, audit trails, money movement, or other high-risk decisions, human sign-off stays in place. Automation can organise the review, but it does not replace the person who has to own the decision.

If the data lives in email, spreadsheets, or someone’s head, clean that up before you think about automation. That is less exciting than “AI everywhere,” but it is usually where the work starts.
